claim: The CRISPR system for prokaryotic adaptive immunity provides RNA-mediated protection from viruses and mobile genetic elements.
source: The CRISPR system for prokaryotic adaptive immunity provides RNA-mediated protection from viruses and mobile genetic elements.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by extensive literature and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: When viral RNA transcripts are detected, type III systems adopt an activated state that licenses DNA interference and synthesis of cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA).
source: When viral RNA transcripts are detected, type III systems adopt an activated state that licenses DNA interference and synthesis of cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing cOA synthesis upon target RNA binding.

claim: cOA activates nucleases and transcription factors that orchestrate the antiviral response.
source: cOA activates nucleases and transcription factors that orchestrate the antiviral response.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental demonstration of Csx1 activation by cOA in the manuscript and by citations to prior work.

claim: cOA synthesis commences on target RNA binding.
source: We demonstrate that cOA synthesis is subject to tight temporal control, commencing on target RNA binding, and is deactivated rapidly as target RNA is cleaved and dissociates.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data showing cOA production in the presence of target RNA and ATP.

claim: cOA synthesis is deactivated rapidly as target RNA is cleaved and dissociates.
source: We demonstrate that cOA synthesis is subject to tight temporal control, commencing on target RNA binding, and is deactivated rapidly as target RNA is cleaved and dissociates.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data showing correlation between target RNA cleavage, dissociation, and cessation of cOA production.

claim: Mismatches in the target RNA are well tolerated and still activate the cyclase domain, except when located close to the 3' end of the target.
source: Mismatches in the target RNA are well tolerated and still activate the cyclase domain, except when located close to the 3' end of the target.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with various mismatch-containing target RNAs showing differential effects on cOA production based on mismatch position.

claim: Phosphorothioate modification reduces target RNA cleavage and stimulates cOA production.
source: Phosphorothioate modification reduces target RNA cleavage and stimulates cOA production.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental comparison of unmodified and phosphorothioate-modified target RNAs.

claim: The 'RNA shredding' activity originally ascribed to type III systems may be a reflection of an exquisite mechanism for control of the Cas10 subunit, rather than a direct antiviral defence.
source: The 'RNA shredding' activity originally ascribed to type III systems may thus be a reflection of an exquisite mechanism for control of the Cas10 subunit, rather than a direct antiviral defence.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data showing correlation between RNA cleavage and deactivation of cOA synthesis.

claim: Class two effector complexes include Cas9, which has seen wide application in genome engineering.
source: Class two effector complexes include Cas9, which has seen wide application in genome engineering.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the CRISPR field.

claim: Class one complexes are multisubunit systems that use a backbone built around Cas7 subunits which binds the crRNA.
source: Class one complexes are more intricate, multisubunit systems that use a backbone built around Cas7 subunits which binds the crRNA.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Class 1 CRISPR systems.

claim: Type I complexes bind target DNA and then recruit the Cas3 enzyme via an interaction with the Cse1 subunit, resulting in Cas3 mediated DNA degradation.
source: The type I complexes, typified by Cascade (type I-E) from Escherichia coli, bind target DNA and then recruit the Cas3 enzyme via an interaction with the Cse1 subunit, resulting in Cas3 mediated DNA degradation (Hochstrasser et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Type III complexes bind invading RNA species, activating several different enzymatic activities present within the complex.
source: In contrast, type III complexes bind invading RNA species, activating several different enzymatic activities present within the complex (reviewed in [Tamulaitis et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The Cas7-mediated 'backbone cleavage' activity degrades bound target RNA with a characteristic 6-nucleotide spacing.
source: The Cas7-mediated 'backbone cleavage' activity degrades bound target RNA with a characteristic 6-nucleotide spacing (Staals et al., 2014; Tamulaitis et al., 2014; Hale et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The HD-nuclease domain of the large Cas10 subunit is responsible for target DNA degradation.
source: The HD-nuclease domain of the large Cas10 subunit is responsible for target DNA degradation (Elmore et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The HD nuclease domain is activated when target RNA is bound by the complex.
source: This is activated when target RNA is bound by the complex (Samai et al., 2015), providing a mechanism for transcription-dependent DNA targeting (Deng et al., 2013) that allows lysogenic phage to persist in the host chromosome (Goldberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Type III CRISPR systems are much more tolerant of mismatches with nucleic acid targets than other types, making viral escape difficult.
source: Type III CRISPR systems are much more tolerant of mismatches with nucleic acid targets than other types, making viral escape difficult (Pyenson et al., 2017; Manica et al., 2011; Manica et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Many type III system operons encode a protein such as Csm6 or Csx1 that is not part of the effector complex.
source: For some time, it was known that many type III system operons encode a protein such as Csm6 or Csx1 that is not part of the effector complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Csm6 and Csx1 genes have been shown to be important for CRISPR-based immunity in vivo.
source: These genes have been shown to be important for CRISPR-based immunity in vivo (Deng et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Csm6 and Csx1 proteins have a CARF domain linked to a HEPN domain and have weak ribonuclease activity in vitro.
source: The proteins have a CARF (CRISPR-associated Rossmann fold) domain linked to a HEPN (higher eukaryotes and prokaryotes nucleotide binding) domain and have weak ribonuclease activity in vitro (Niewoehner and Jinek, 2016; Sheppard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CARF domains were predicted to bind some form of cyclic nucleotide, perhaps as an allosteric effector.
source: CARF domains were predicted to bind some form of cyclic nucleotide, perhaps as an allosteric effector (Lintner et al., 2011) but the source of the effector was unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The cyclase domain of Cas10 can synthesise cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) molecules from ATP, when activated by target RNA binding.
source: This puzzle was solved when it was demonstrated that the cyclase domain of Cas10 can synthesise cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) molecules from ATP, when activated by target RNA binding (Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Niewoehner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: cOA species consist of 3 to 6 membered rings of AMP with 3' and 5' linkages and have not been observed in any other biological context.
source: cOA species consist of 3 to 6 membered rings of AMP with 3' and 5' linkages and have not been observed in any other biological context.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on prior characterization of cOA molecules.

claim: cOA binds to and activates Csm6 and Csx1, enhancing their ribonuclease activity.
source: cOA in turn binds to and activates Csm6 and Csx1, enhancing their ribonuclease activity.
evidence: This is supported by prior work and demonstrated in this manuscript.

claim: cOA represents a new type of second messenger, generated by type III CRISPR effector complexes, that sculpts the cellular response to invasion by MGE.
source: cOA thus represents a new type of second messenger, generated by type III CRISPR effector complexes, that sculpts the cellular response to invasion by MGE (reviewed in [Koonin and Makarova, 2018]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: S. solfataricus encodes two type III effector systems: a Cmr (type III-B) complex and a Csm (type III-D) complex.
source: S. solfataricus encodes two type III effector systems: a Cmr (type III-B) complex, which has a unique Cmr7 subunit (Zhang et al., 2012), and a Csm (type III-D) complex (Rouillon et al., 2013) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both Cmr and Csm complexes have a Cas7 backbone and a large Cas10 subunit with HD and cyclase domains, but they differ in their structural organisation and nuclease activities.
source: Both have a Cas7 backbone and a large Cas10 subunit with HD and cyclase domains, but they differ in their structural organisation and nuclease activities (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: S. solfataricus Cmr has two distinct target RNA cleavage modes and has not been observed to cleave DNA targets.
source: S. solfataricus Cmr has two distinct target RNA cleavage modes and has not been observed to cleave DNA targets (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The S. solfataricus Csm complex has the canonical Cas7-mediated 'backbone' target RNA cleavage activity and a DNA nuclease activity.
source: In contrast the Csm complex has the canonical Cas7-mediated 'backbone' target RNA cleavage activity and a DNA nuclease activity (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The S. solfataricus CRISPR system has six CRISPR-associated CARF-domain proteins.
source: The S. solfataricus CRISPR system also has six CRISPR-associated CARF-domain proteins of which one is predicted to be HEPN nucleases (Sso1389), two belong to the Csa3-like transcription factor family (Sso1444 and 1445) and three have indeterminate function (Sso1393, 1397 and 2081) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and represents bioinformatic analysis.

claim: S. solfataricus can mount a sophisticated and wide-ranging antiviral response through cOA signalling.
source: This suggests that S. solfataricus can mount a sophisticated and wide-ranging antiviral response through cOA signalling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of multiple CARF-domain proteins.

claim: Large-scale changes in gene expression on viral infection in S. solfataricus have been reported.
source: Large-scale changes in gene expression on viral infection in S. solfataricus have been reported (Quax et al., 2013), which may be at least partly due to cOA signalling.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work, with speculation about the role of cOA.

claim: cOA synthesis has not been directly demonstrated in any type III system in the archaea prior to this study.
source: However, to date, cOA synthesis has not been directly demonstrated in any type III system in the archaea.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: A HEPN family Csx1 nuclease from S. islandicus was shown to be activated by mRNA with a 3' polyadenylate tail.
source: Recently, a HEPN family Csx1 nuclease from the related organism S. islandicus was shown to be activated by mRNA with a 3' polyadenylate tail (Han et al., 2017b), which opens another possible mechanism for activation of this antiviral response, independent of cOA signalling.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Viral infection induces dormancy in S. islandicus.
source: Furthermore, viral infection induces dormancy in S. islandicus (Bautista et al., 2015), which could be consistent with activation of a cOA-dependent ribonuclease or cOA-dependent changes in transcription.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The S. solfataricus Csm/III-D complex generates cOA in response to target RNA binding.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the S. solfataricus Csm/III-D complex generates cOA in response to target RNA binding, activating a CARF-domain nuclease Csx1 for RNA degradation.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The S. solfataricus Csm complex activates the CARF-domain nuclease Csx1 for RNA degradation.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the S. solfataricus Csm/III-D complex generates cOA in response to target RNA binding, activating a CARF-domain nuclease Csx1 for RNA degradation.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data showing Csx1 activation by cOA.

claim: cOA4 is the relevant activator for Csx1.
source: We describe a new method to generate short oligoadenosine molecules with a 3'-cyclic phosphate moiety and use this to determine that cOA4 is the relevant activator for Csx1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with MazF-generated linear oligoadenylates.

claim: Activation of cOA synthesis is sensitive to changes at the 3' end of RNA targets, next to Cas10.
source: Activation of cOA synthesis is sensitive to changes at the 3' end of RNA targets, next to Cas10.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with mismatch-containing and truncated target RNAs.

claim: The deactivation of cOA synthesis correlates with backbone cleavage towards the centre of bound target RNA, leading to rapid product release.
source: The deactivation of cOA synthesis is shown to correlate with backbone cleavage towards the centre of bound target RNA, leading to rapid product release.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic analysis of RNA cleavage, product release, and cOA synthesis.

claim: The wild-type Csm complex can bind and cleave target RNA via 'backbone-mediated' cleavage by the Cas7 subunit.
source: Using a radioactively labelled target RNA, we first confirmed that the wild-type Csm complex can bind and cleave the target RNA via 'backbone-mediated' cleavage by the Cas7 subunit (Figure 2A), as demonstrated previously (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 2A and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Three cleavage sites (B1-B3) are clearly visible in the Csm backbone cleavage assay, and a fourth (B4) is very faint.
source: Three cleavage sites (B1-B3) are clearly visible, and a fourth (B4) is very faint.
evidence: This is observed in the gel shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Targeted mutations that abrogate the active site of the HD domain and cyclase domain did not affect backbone cleavage.
source: Targeted mutations that abrogate the active site of the HD domain and cyclase domain (denoted HD and GGDD, respectively) did not affect this backbone cleavage mode.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 2A showing similar cleavage patterns for wild-type and mutant complexes.

claim: The presence of 1 mM ATP in backbone cleavage reactions had little effect on activity.
source: The presence of 1 mM ATP in these reactions also had little effect on activity.
evidence: This is observed in the gel shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cleavage of the target RNA by Csx1 was only observed with products of reactions that had included ATP as well as Csm with a wild-type cyclase domain.
source: Cleavage of the target RNA by Csx1 at five positions (arrowed) was only observed with products of reactions that had included ATP as well as Csm with a wild-type cyclase domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 2B.

claim: An active Csm HD domain was not required for stimulation of Csx1.
source: An active Csm HD domain was not required for stimulation of Csx1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 2B showing Csx1 activation with the HD mutant.

claim: Csx1 is activated by a small molecule that is synthesised by the cyclase domain of Csm when it is incubated with target RNA in the presence of ATP.
source: These data suggest that Csx1 is activated by a small molecule that is synthesised by the cyclase domain of Csm when it is incubated with target RNA in the presence of ATP, consistent with an active cOA-signalling pathway in S. solfataricus.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing Csx1 activation only when Csm with active cyclase is incubated with target RNA and ATP.

claim: Csm synthesizes small radioactive oligomers when incubated with target RNA and α-32P-ATP, dependent on an active cyclase domain.
source: By carrying out the reaction shown in Figure 2A in the presence of α-32P-ATP, followed by separation of reaction products by denaturing gel electrophoresis, we observed synthesis of small radioactive oligomers, dependent on an active Csm cyclase domain, consistent with cOA synthesis by the Csm complex (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 2C.

claim: The major product of Csm cyclase activity corresponds to cOA4, with much lower amounts of other cyclic molecules present.
source: Liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (LC-MS) was used to confirm that the major product corresponded to cOA4, with much lower amounts of other cyclic molecules present (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Csx1 cleavage sites map to C/U dinucleotides for the substrate A1.
source: The cleavage sites map to C/U dinucleotides for this substrate (see Table 1).
evidence: This is determined by analysis of the cleavage pattern and substrate sequence.

claim: MazF can be used to generate linear oligoadenylates with a 2',3'-cyclic phosphate terminus.
source: In order to generate large quantities of defined signalling species, we have devised a convenient method for the generation of linear polyadenylates with a 2',3' cyclic phosphate – a species that has an identical mass to the corresponding cOA. To do this, we took advantage of the specificity of the MazF toxin of E. coli, which cuts RNA 5' to an ACA recognition sequence, leaving a 2',3'-cyclic phosphate (Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 3A and supported by citation about MazF specificity.

claim: Linear A4 >P oligoadenylate activates Csx1 nuclease activity comparably to authentic cOA mixture generated by Csm.
source: We observed clear activation of the Csx1 ribonuclease activity by A4 >P, comparable to the activation by the authentic cOA mixture generated by the S. solfataricus Csm effector, demonstrating that cOA4 is the relevant activator for this enzyme.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 3B showing similar Csx1 activation by A4>P and authentic cOA.

claim: Under single turnover conditions, Csm-mediated backbone cleavage at sites B1-B3 of a transcript target sequence could be observed.
source: Under single turnover conditions (Csm 5 µM, transcript 5 nM), Csm-mediated backbone cleavage at sites B1-B3 of the transcript target sequence could be observed both by the processing of the large RNA species from 205 down to 170 nt, and by the appearance of small RNA products corresponding to cleavage at sites B1 and B2 further down the gel (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 4A.

claim: The rate of transcript cleavage by Csm is kc = 0.15 ± 0.01 min−1.
source: We quantified the fractional cleavage of the transcript over time and fitted it to an exponential equation, yielding a rate kc = 0. 15 ± 0.01 min−1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is determined by quantitative analysis of the gel data in Figure 4.

claim: cOA synthesis was observed from early time points and plateaued over the time course of the transcript cleavage reaction.
source: cOA synthesis was observed from early time points and plateaued over the time course.
evidence: This is observed in the gel and quantification shown in Figure 4.

claim: As the target site in the transcript RNA becomes fully cleaved between 20 and 40 min, cOA4 production shuts down.
source: As the target site in the transcript RNA becomes fully cleaved between 20 and 40 min, cOA4 production shuts down.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the bar chart in Figure 4B showing decreased cOA production rate.

claim: When target RNA is complementary to the 5' handle of the crRNA sequence, or when the 5 nt mismatched 3'-end of target RNA is missing, backbone cleavage still occurs but the cyclase domain is not activated.
source: When the target RNA is complementary to the 5' handle of the crRNA sequence, or when the 5 nt mismatched 3'-end of target RNA is missing, backbone cleavage still occurs but the cyclase domain is not activated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gels in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: All mismatched targets tested were still cleaved by Csm.
source: All mismatched targets were still cleaved by Csm, in keeping with previous observations (Staals et al., 2014; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gels in Figure 5 and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Target MM1 and MM2, with two mismatches spanning cleavage site B1 and B2 respectively, abolished backbone cleavage at the mutated position.
source: Target MM1 and MM2, with two mismatches spanning cleavage site B1 and B2 respectively, abolished backbone cleavage at the mutated position, but cleavage at other sites was still observed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 5A.

claim: None of the double mismatches introduced 5' to site B1 on the target RNA reduced cOA synthesis.
source: None of the double mismatches introduced 5' to site B1 on the target RNA reduced cOA synthesis, showing that they behave very similarly to fully cognate target RNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 5A showing cOA production with these substrates.

claim: A double mismatch positioned two nt (MM0.5) or four nt (MM1) from the 3' end of the matching target RNA resulted in complete abolition of cOA synthesis.
source: In contrast, a double mismatch positioned two nt (MM0.5) or four nt (MM1) from the 3' end of the matching target RNA resulted in complete abolition of cOA synthesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 5A showing no cOA production with these substrates.

claim: Csm is particularly sensitive to disruptions of targets at the 3' end nearest the Cas10 subunit, whether by truncation, base-pairing with the crRNA 5'-handle, or mismatch.
source: Together, these data suggest that Csm is particularly sensitive to disruptions of targets at the 3' end nearest the Cas10 subunit, whether by truncation, base-pairing with the crRNA 5'-handle, or mismatch (discussed later).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on various target RNA modifications.

claim: Site B1, which is the closest site to the Cas10 subunit, was cleaved with a rate constant kB1 of 0.19 min−1.
source: Site B1, which is the closest site to the Cas10 subunit, was cleaved with a rate constant kB1 of 0.19 min−1 under these conditions.
evidence: This is determined by quantitative analysis of the gel data in Figure 6.

claim: The backbone cleavage site B2 was cut with a rate kB2 = 0.077 min−1.
source: The next backbone cleavage site, B2, was cut about half as fast (kB2 = 0.077 min−1).
evidence: This is determined by quantitative analysis of the gel data in Figure 6.

claim: The third backbone cleavage site B3, distal to Cas10, was cleaved at the slowest rate (kB3 = 0.004 min−1).
source: The third site, distal to Cas10, was cleaved at the slowest rate (kB3 = 0.004 min−1).
evidence: This is determined by quantitative analysis of the gel data in Figure 6.

claim: Faster target RNA cleavage at sites closer to the Cas10 domain has been observed qualitatively for other type III systems and may be a general phenomenon.
source: Faster target RNA cleavage at sites closer to the Cas10 domain has been observed qualitatively for other type III systems (Staals et al., 2014; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), and may be a general phenomenon.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the data in this manuscript.

claim: The rate of cOA4 synthesis peaked at 10 min and rapidly fell away.
source: The rate of cOA4 synthesis peaked at 10 min and rapidly fell away, suggesting that the cyclase domain is rapidly activated on target RNA binding, and quickly deactivated after target RNA cleavage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Under single turnover conditions with 25 nM target RNA, very low amounts of cOA4 production were observed after 20 min of reaction.
source: Under single turnover conditions with 25 nM target RNA, we observed very low amounts of cOA4 production after 20 min of reaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 7B.

claim: When target RNA was increased ten-fold, cOA production continued for a longer period.
source: When the target RNA was increased ten-fold, this allowed cOA production to continue for a longer period.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 7B.

claim: cOA synthesis is closely linked to target RNA availability, and is rapidly deactivated once target RNA is cleaved.
source: Thus, cOA synthesis is closely linked to target RNA availability, and is rapidly deactivated once target RNA is cleaved.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 7B showing dependence on target RNA concentration.

claim: The phosphorothioate target RNA was still cleaved by Csm, but the rate was significantly slower.
source: The P-thioate target RNA was still cleaved by Csm, but the rate was significantly slower (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of cleavage rates in Figure 8A.

claim: A defect in cleavage at site B2 was apparent with phosphorothioate target RNA.
source: In particular, a defect in cleavage at site B2 was apparent.
evidence: This is observed in the gel in Figure 8A.

claim: cOA4 production was strongly enhanced in the reaction with phosphorothioate target RNA.
source: This revealed that cOA4 production was strongly enhanced in the reaction with P-thioate target RNA, consistent with a requirement for cleavage and/or dissociation of cleaved target RNA to switch off the activity of the Cyclase domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel and quantification in Figure 8.

claim: The rate of dissociation of cleaved target RNA is koff = 0.066 ± 0.003 min−1.
source: The rate of cleaved target RNA release was determined as koff = 0.066 ± 0.003 min−1 (Figure 9B), similar to the rate of cleavage of site B2 in the centre of the target RNA (kB2 = 0.077 min−1), significantly faster than the cleavage at site B3.
evidence: This is determined by quantitative analysis of the native gel data in Figure 9.

claim: The site of cleavage of the main dissociated product was confirmed as B2 using a synthetic RNA marker.
source: The site of cleavage of the main dissociated product was confirmed as B2 using a synthetic RNA marker of that size (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The clearance of target RNA from the Csm complex may be governed by the rate of backbone cleavage rather than product dissociation.
source: Thus, the clearance of target RNA from the Csm complex may be governed by the rate of backbone cleavage rather than product dissociation.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of cleavage and dissociation rates.

claim: Cleavage up to the centre of the target RNA (site B2) appears sufficient to allow product dissociation.
source: Furthermore, cleavage up to the centre of the target RNA (site B2) appears sufficient to allow product dissociation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the dissociated product corresponds to B2 cleavage.

claim: The rate of cOA synthesis decrease fits an exponential with a rate constant kobs = 0.047 ± 0.008 min−1.
source: We also analysed the rate of synthesis of cOA4 over time (as shown in Figure 7), setting the rate at 10 min equal to one and normalising the data. The data fit a simple exponential with a rate constant kobs = 0.047 ± 0.008 min−1.
evidence: This is determined by quantitative analysis of the cOA synthesis data.

claim: The rates of target RNA cleavage at site B2, RNA product dissociation and inactivation of cOA synthesis were very similar, within experimental error.
source: In conclusion, the rates of target RNA cleavage at site B2, RNA product dissociation and inactivation of cOA synthesis were very similar, within experimental error.
evidence: This is a summary of the kinetic data comparing the three rates.

claim: When cleavage at site B2 is perturbed by phosphorothioate modification, cOA production is enhanced significantly.
source: When cleavage at site B2 is perturbed by phosphorothioate modification, cOA production is enhanced significantly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 8.

claim: Activation of the cyclase domain occurs quickly upon target RNA binding, followed by deactivation as target RNA is cleaved and dissociates from the Csm complex.
source: These observations are consistent with activation of the cyclase domain quickly upon target RNA binding, followed by deactivation as target RNA is cleaved and dissociates from the Csm complex.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the kinetic data.

claim: The type III-D Csm complex from S. solfataricus generates cOA on binding target RNA.
source: We have demonstrated that the type III-D Csm complex from S. solfataricus generates cOA on binding target RNA.
evidence: This is the main finding of the manuscript, demonstrated by multiple experiments.

claim: Given the preponderance of CARF-family proteins associated with type III systems and the conservation of the cyclase domain, cOA synthesis is likely to be a general phenomenon.
source: Given the preponderance of CARF-family proteins associated with type III systems and the conservation of the cyclase domain, this is likely to be a general phenomenon.
evidence: This is an inference based on bioinformatic analysis and the data presented.

claim: The generation of cOA4 by S. solfataricus Csm fits with the binding pocket modelled for the CARF domain of the transcription factor Csa3.
source: For the S. solfataricus system, the generation of cOA4 fits with the binding pocket modelled for the CARF domain of the transcription factor Csa3 (Lintner et al., 2011), and with the observation that OA4 activates the CARF nuclease Csx1 in the related organism S. islandicus (Han et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the data in this manuscript.

claim: Enterococcus italicus Csm generates mostly cOA6, and this molecule is the effector for the corresponding Csm6 enzyme.
source: Enterococcus italicus Csm generates mostly cOA6, and this molecule is the effector for the corresponding Csm6 enzyme (Niewoehner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The major product generated by the S. thermophilus enzyme is cOA3, despite the fact that the corresponding Csm6 protein is activated by cOA6.
source: In contrast, the major product generated by the S. thermophilus enzyme is cOA3, despite the fact that the corresponding Csm6 protein is activated by cOA6 (Kazlauskiene et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CARF domains are formed by dimeric subunits, and the corresponding activators are likely to have a 2-fold axis of symmetry.
source: Given that CARF domains are formed by dimeric subunits, the corresponding activators are likely to have a 2-fold axis of symmetry, which fits with observations that cOA4 and cOA6 are both activators of CARF nucleases.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge and experimental observations.

claim: cOA3 and cOA5 lack 2-fold symmetry and are unlikely to bind to CARF domains.
source: In contrast, cOA3 and cOA5 lack this symmetry and are unlikely to bind to CARF domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural considerations.

claim: cOA3 and cOA5 may be irrelevant in the context of signalling by type III systems, or alternatively may be activators for families of effector proteins that utilise a different domain for ligand binding.
source: They may be irrelevant in the context of signalling by type III systems, or alternatively may be activators for families of effector proteins that utilise a different domain for ligand binding.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential roles of these molecules.

claim: Target RNA binding has been shown to activate both the HD nuclease and cOA synthesis activities of diverse type III systems.
source: Target RNA binding has been shown to activate both the HD nuclease and cOA synthesis activities of diverse type III systems.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work and confirmed in this manuscript.

claim: Target RNA binding likely results in conformational changes in the complex, and the Cas10 subunit in particular.
source: This is likely to result from conformational changes in the complex, and the Cas10 subunit in particular.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of activation.

claim: A 5° rotation of the Cas10 subunit on target RNA binding has been observed for T. thermophilus Cmr.
source: A 5° rotation of the Cas10 subunit on target RNA binding has been observed for T. thermophilus Cmr (Taylor et al., 2015), which may reflect this activation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The activation of cOA synthesis is rapid, with activity detected within the first minute of incubation of Csm with target RNA transcripts.
source: We observe that the activation of cOA synthesis is rapid, with activity detected within the first minute of incubation of Csm with target RNA transcripts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time course data in Figure 4.

claim: Activation of cOA synthesis requires a 3' extension to the target RNA that does not base-pair with the 5'-handle of the crRNA.
source: As for S. thermophilus Csm, activation requires a 3' extension to the target RNA that does not base-pair with the 5'-handle of the crRNA (Figure 5 and [Kazlauskiene et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5 and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In standard oligonucleotide substrates there is a 5 nt 3'-overhang, which fits the minimum requirement predicted from biochemical and modelling studies.
source: In our standard oligonucleotide substrates there is a 5 nt 3'- overhang, which fits the minimum requirement predicted from the biochemical and modelling study of the Siksnys group (Kazlauskiene et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A short stretch of RNA at the 3' end presumably interacts with the Cas10 and/or the Csm4 subunit in such a way that a conformational change occurs, resulting in activation of both the HD nuclease and GGDD cyclase active sites.
source: This short stretch of RNA presumably interacts with the Cas10 and/or the Csm4 subunit in such a way that a conformational change occurs in this region of the complex, resulting in the activation of both the HD nuclease and GGDD cyclase active sites, paving the way for DNA degradation and, through cOA signalling, the activation of HEPN family ribonucleases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and structural considerations.

claim: There is a high degree of tolerance for mismatches in target RNAs in type III systems.
source: As observed for other type III systems, there is a high degree of tolerance for mismatches in target RNAs (Pyenson et al., 2017; Manica et al., 2011, 2013; Goldberg et al., 2018), which all tend to be cleaved, and thus removed from the enzyme.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by the data in this manuscript.

claim: 2 nt mismatches 5' to site B1 activate the cyclase domain and would elicit a full anti-viral response.
source: By extending this analysis to examine cOA synthesis, we observe that 2 nt mismatches 5' to site B1 do activate the cyclase domain and would thus elicit a full anti-viral response.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5.

claim: Target RNAs with a double mismatch at or 3' to site B1 (within 4–5 nt of the 3' end of target RNA base-paired with the crRNA), whilst still cleaved, did not activate cOA production.
source: However, the target RNAs with a double mismatch at or 3' to site B1 (corresponding to positions within 4–5 nt of the 3' end of target RNA base-paired with the crRNA), whilst still cleaved, did not activate cOA production (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5.

claim: There is an important role for the 3' end of the bound target RNA close to the Cas10 subunit where sequence requirements are more stringent.
source: This suggests an important role for the 3' end of the bound target RNA close to the Cas10 subunit where sequence requirements are more stringent.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of mismatches at different positions.

claim: Destabilization of the RNA duplex near the 3' end can lead to changes in the conformation of the single-stranded 3' end of the target RNA, resulting in failure to activate the cyclase domain.
source: Presumably, destabilization of the RNA duplex in this region can lead to changes in the conformation of the single-stranded 3' end of the target RNA, resulting in failure to activate the cyclase domain.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Viral targets that manage to mutate in the key 3' area may have more chance of escaping from cOA-mediated HEPN nuclease activation.
source: Viral targets that manage to mutate in this key area may thus have more chance of escaping from cOA-mediated HEPN nuclease activation, which is a key determinant of type III CRISPR immunity.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary implications of the findings.

claim: Substantial blocks of mismatches in the 3' area do not prevent phage targeting by the S. epidermidis type III-A system.
source: In contrast, substantial blocks of mismatches in this general area do not prevent phage targeting by the S. epidermidis type III-A system (Pyenson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Differences in mismatch tolerance could be due to differences between the activation of the cyclase and HD nuclease domains of Cas10, or to differences between type III-A and III-D systems.
source: This could be due to differences between the activation of the cyclase and HD nuclease domains of Cas10, or to differences between type III-A and III-D systems and deserves further analysis.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for observed differences.

claim: The Marraffini group reports that Csm6 selectively targets phage transcripts.
source: The Marraffini group report that Csm6 selectively targets phage transcripts (Jiang et al., 2016), and the spatial coupling of the HD nuclease activity of Cas10 to actively transcribing viral RNA targets could ensure at least partial selectivity for foreign nucleic acids.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It seems likely that host nucleic acids would be caught in the cross-fire of the antiviral attack, leading to a shutdown in host gene expression or even cell death.
source: Nonetheless, it seems likely that host nucleic acids would be caught in the cross-fire of this 'scorched earth' attack, leading to a shutdown in host gene expression or even cell death – which, as pointed out previously, could be a sensible option if viral infection is established in the cell (Elmore et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Viral infection has been shown to result in dormancy and cell death in S. islandicus, which harbours a type III CRISPR system.
source: Indeed, viral infection has been shown to result in dormancy and cell death in S. islandicus, which harbours a type III CRISPR system (Bautista et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The activation of the HD nuclease and cyclase domains of Cas10 as a result of target RNA binding is not an irreversible event.
source: The activation of the HD nuclease and cyclase domains of Cas10 as a result of target RNA binding is not an irreversible event.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data showing deactivation of cOA synthesis.

claim: These domains could be deactivated either when target RNA is cleaved, or when it dissociates from the complex, with a time lag possible in either circumstance.
source: Logically, it could be predicted that these domains are deactivated either when target RNA is cleaved, or when it dissociates from the complex, with a time lag possible in either circumstance.
evidence: This is logical reasoning about possible mechanisms.

claim: Backbone cleavage of RNA was the first activity detected in type III CRISPR systems, and appears to be ubiquitous.
source: Backbone cleavage of RNA was the first activity detected in type III CRISPR systems (Hale et al., 2009), and appears to be ubiquitous.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Backbone cleavage activity is not essential for type III-mediated immunity against phage infection in vivo.
source: Nonetheless, this activity is not essential for type III-mediated immunity against phage infection in vivo (Samai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Terns and colleagues suggested that target RNA cleavage may represent a means for deactivation of the DNA nuclease activity of type III systems.
source: Terns and colleagues suggested that target RNA cleavage may represent a means for deactivation of the DNA nuclease activity of type III systems, as cleavage of the RNA transcript would cause the type III effector to 'drift away' (Elmore et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It seems more likely that target RNA cleavage and subsequent dissociation allows a collapse back to an inactive ground state of Cas10, switching off the HD nuclease and cOA signalling activities.
source: Rather than spatial separation though, it seems more likely that target RNA cleavage and subsequent dissociation allows a collapse back to an inactive ground state of Cas10, switching off the highly potent HD nuclease and cOA signalling activities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Csm (III-A) complex from S. thermophilus and Thermus thermophilus appear to cut target RNA first at the 3' end nearest the Cas10 subunit.
source: The Csm (III-A) complex from S. thermophilus and Thermus thermophilus also appear to cut target RNA first at the 3' end nearest the Cas10 subunit (Staals et al., 2014; Tamulaitis et al., 2014), and cleavage by S. thermophilus Csm is rapid – of the order of 5 s under single turnover conditions (Kazlauskiene et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Thermatoga maritima Cmr (III-B) cleaves target RNA with six nt spacing at four sites, with cleavage fastest at site 2, which is 11 nt from the 3' end of the target RNA.
source: Thermatoga maritima Cmr (III-B) cleaves target RNA with six nt spacing at four sites, with cleavage fastest at site 2, which is 11 nt from the 3' end of the target RNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cleavage by T. maritima Cmr is rapid under single turnover conditions, reaching completion within 1 min for site 2 and 5 min for site 4.
source: Cleavage is rapid under single turnover conditions, reaching completion within 1 min for site 2 and 5 min for site 4, which is 23 nt from the 3' end (Estrella et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The rate of product release has not previously been quantified in any type III system.
source: The rate of product release has not previously been quantified in any system.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: For S. thermophilus Csm, multiple turnover kinetic experiments suggested that product dissociation, whilst rate limiting, was moderately fast (k = 3 min−1).
source: For S. thermophilus Csm, multiple turnover kinetic experiments suggested that product dissociation, whilst rate limiting, was moderately fast (k = 3 min−1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Activation of the DNase activity of the HD domain of S. thermophilus Csm persisted over a much longer timescale, 30–60 min.
source: However, activation of the DNase activity of the HD domain persisted over a much longer timescale, 30–60 min.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The authors of the S. thermophilus study suggested that the activated state of Csm persists after target RNA dissociation.
source: The authors suggested that the activated state of S. thermophilus Csm persists after target RNA dissociation (Kazlauskiene et al., 2016), but an alternative is that there is heterogeneity in the population of Csm enzymes, with some remaining bound to RNA targets and hence preserved in an active state for much longer periods than others.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work, with an alternative interpretation offered.

claim: For T. maritima Cmr, cleaved target RNA dissociation correlated with the deactivation of the HD nuclease domain, although the rates were not measured.
source: For T. maritima Cmr, cleaved target RNA dissociation also correlated with the deactivation of the HD nuclease domain, although the rates were not measured (Estrella et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Comparatively rapid cleavage occurs at sites B1 (0.19 min−1) and B2 (0.08 min−1), nearest to the 3' end of the target RNA and proximal to the Cas10 subunit, and much slower cleavage of more distal sites.
source: We observed comparatively rapid cleavage at sites B1 (0.19 min−1) and B2 (0.08 min−1), nearest to the 3' end of the target RNA and proximal to the Cas10 subunit, and much slower cleavage of more distal sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the kinetic data in Figure 6.

claim: The trend for faster cleavage at the 3' end is clear from studies of other type III systems.
source: The trend for faster cleavage at the 3' end is clear from studies of other type III systems.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The overall cleavage rate of a transcript RNA was very similar to the rate observed with oligonucleotide substrates.
source: The overall cleavage rate of a transcript RNA, which is a more physiologically relevant target, was very similar (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of the data in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: A highly significant increase in cOA production was noted with phosphorothioate-modified substrates, consistent with a link between target RNA cleavage and cOA synthesis.
source: The introduction of phosphorothioate linkages spanning sites B1 and B2 reduced but did not abolish target RNA cleavage (Figure 8), and we noted a highly significant increase in cOA production with these substrates, consistent with a link between target RNA cleavage and cOA synthesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 8.

claim: Full target RNA digestion may not be required for product release.
source: Thus, it appears that full target RNA digestion may not be required for product release.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the dissociated product corresponds to B2 cleavage, not B3.

claim: RNA dissociation is likely not rate limiting; rather, the chemical step of RNA cleavage determines the rate of product release.
source: Furthermore, RNA dissociation is likely not rate limiting. Rather, the chemical step of RNA cleavage determines the rate of product release.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of cleavage and dissociation rates.

claim: RNA duplexes of around 20 bp would be only marginally stable at 70°C in the absence of stabilising protein interactions.
source: As our assays were carried out at 70°C, close to the growth temperature of S. solfataricus, RNA duplexes of around 20 bp would be only marginally stable in the absence of stabilising protein interactions.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of RNA duplex stability at high temperature.

claim: In S. islandicus, target RNA forming less than 20 bp with the crRNA was observed to dissociate.
source: This fits the situation in S. islandicus, where target RNA forming less than 20 bp with the crRNA was observed to dissociate (Han et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Target RNA cleavage products tend to accumulate under single turnover conditions rather than undergoing processive cleavage to the smallest possible products in type III systems.
source: It is also consistent with the general observation for type III systems that target RNA cleavage products tend to accumulate under single turnover conditions rather than undergoing processive cleavage to the smallest possible products (Staals et al., 2014; Tamulaitis et al., 2014; Hale et al., 2014; Han et al., 2017a; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RNA cleavage and dissociation results in the simultaneous deactivation of the cyclase domain, presumably due to rapid conformational change to the ground state.
source: Finally, RNA cleavage and dissociation results in the simultaneous deactivation of the cyclase domain, presumably due to rapid conformational change to the ground state.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing correlation between these events.

claim: Target RNA cleavage (and therefore dissociation) in type III systems functions as an 'off switch' for the cyclase and HD nuclease active sites.
source: These observations are consistent with the hypothesis that target RNA cleavage (and therefore dissociation) in type III systems functions as an 'off switch' for the cyclase and HD nuclease active sites (Estrella et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The primary role of target RNA cleavage may be to function as an 'off switch' rather than the protective effect of direct degradation of viral transcripts.
source: This, rather than the protective effect of direct degradation of viral transcripts, may be the primary role of target RNA cleavage.
evidence: This is speculation based on the data and interpretation.

claim: A single target RNA may trigger synthesis of many molecules of cOA, which in turn would activate multiple HEPN ribonucleases for active RNA degradation – a potent amplification of antiviral defences.
source: After all, a single target RNA may trigger synthesis of many molecules of cOA, which in turn would activate multiple HEPN ribonucleases for active RNA degradation – a potent amplification of antiviral defences.
evidence: This is an inference about the amplification mechanism of the system.

claim: Under multiple turnover conditions that may be more reflective of a high viral load in the cell, the cyclase domain is activated for longer periods.
source: Under multiple turnover conditions that may be more reflective of a high viral load in the cell, the cyclase domain is activated for longer periods (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 7.

claim: RNA substrates that are not bona fide targets are still cleaved and thus cleared from the binding site, but do not activate cOA synthesis.
source: RNA substrates that are not bona fide targets are still cleaved and thus cleared from the binding site, but do not activate cOA synthesis, allowing the Csm complex to seek other targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing differential activation by different target RNAs.

claim: Several studies have reported that the HD nuclease activity of type III systems persists up to 1 hr, despite target RNA cleavage reaching completion within a few minutes.
source: Several studies have reported that the HD nuclease activity of type III systems persists up to 1 hr, despite target RNA cleavage reaching completion within a few minutes (Tamulaitis et al., 2014; Estrella et al., 2016; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The HD nuclease and cyclase domains may experience different half-lives in the activated state, with the HD nuclease persisting for much longer.
source: This raises the possibility that the HD nuclease and cyclase domains experience different half-lives in the activated state, with the former persisting for much longer.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations from prior work.

claim: It could make sense to switch off the cyclase activity quickly, as the resultant cOA would provide a much more persistent activation of CARF-family nucleases and transcription factors.
source: It could make sense to switch off the cyclase activity quickly, as the resultant cOA would provide a much more persistent activation of CARF-family nucleases and transcription factors.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional logic of the system.

claim: The removal of the cOA second messenger by an as-yet unidentified phosphodiesterase is likely to play an important part in the control of type III systems.
source: Ultimately, the removal of the cOA second messenger by an as-yet unidentified phosphodiesterase is likely to play an important part in the control of type III systems.
evidence: This is speculation about an unidentified component of the system.
